title: How Long Should a Sermon Be
subtitle: An honest answer to how long a sermon should be, weighing attention, faithfulness to the text, and congregational context against the false comfort of a fixed number.

sections.title: Length Is the Wrong Thing to Ask First
sections.body:
Every young preacher wants a number. Twenty minutes. Thirty. Forty five. The number is a trap.

The question how long should a sermon be sounds practical and is actually a dodge. It treats time as the variable to manage when time is only ever the byproduct of something deeper. A sermon is not long or short. It is full or empty, alive or dead, and a dead sermon of fifteen minutes is longer than a living one of fifty. We have all sat under both. We have all preached both.

So before you ask how long, ask whether every minute is earning its place. The real failure is almost never that a sermon was too long in clock time. It is that it was too long for its content, padded with repetition and throat clearing and stories that went nowhere. Fix the fullness and the length mostly takes care of itself. Chase the number and you will trim the wrong things and keep the fat.

sections.title: What Attention Actually Allows
sections.body:
There is a real ceiling, and it is not a myth, but it is not a stopwatch either.

People can attend to a thing for as long as the thing rewards their attention. That is the whole law of it. A congregation will follow a preacher for forty minutes if every turn pays them back with something they did not have before. They will check out of a fifteen minute sermon the moment they sense the well is dry. Attention is not a fixed tank that empties on a schedule. It is a trust that is renewed or spent with every paragraph.

This means the burden is on the preacher, not the pew. When people drift, the temptation is to blame the phones, the culture, the shrinking attention span of the age. Resist it. The drift is usually feedback. It means the sermon stopped paying, that you coasted, repeated, wandered, said in five minutes what needed two. The disciplined preacher reads the room and learns. Where did I lose them. The honest answer is rarely they cannot focus. The honest answer is usually I stopped giving them a reason to.

sections.title: Let the Text Set the Clock
sections.body:
The length of the sermon should serve the text, not a slot on the bulletin.

Some passages are deep wells. A dense chapter of Romans, a hard saying of Jesus, a psalm that moves through grief to hope, may need every minute you can give it and still leave more unsaid. Other texts are sharp and singular, a single proverb, a brief command, and to stretch them to a fixed length is to drown them in words they never asked for. Faithfulness sometimes means going long. It also sometimes means stopping early because you have said what the text says and the rest would be filler.

This is the discipline most of us lack. We have a length we always preach, and we either inflate a thin text to reach it or compress a rich one to fit it. Both betray the passage. The aim is to say what this text says, no more and no less, and to take exactly the time that requires. A sermon should end when the text has been preached, not when the clock says so and not when you have finally run out of things to add.

sections.title: The Congregation in Front of You
sections.body:
There is no universal right length, because there is no universal congregation.

A people raised on long expository preaching will sit gladly through fifty minutes and feel shortchanged by twenty five. A congregation new to the faith, a room full of skeptics and seekers, a service built around outreach, may be served far better by a tight twenty five that lands clean than by an hour that loses half the room by the midpoint. The same forty minute sermon is generous in one room and self indulgent in another. Wisdom reads the room it is actually in.

This is not compromise. It is love. Paul became all things to all people that he might save some, and the preacher who refuses to consider his hearers has confused stubbornness with conviction. Know who is in front of you. Know what they can receive. Know the difference between the discomfort of being convicted, which is good, and the fatigue of being worn out by a man who would not stop, which is your fault. Preach to the room God gave you, not to the room you wish you had.

sections.title: The Only Answer That Holds
sections.body:
So here is the answer, and it will not fit on a card. As long as it takes to preach the text, and not one minute longer.

That answer refuses the number because the number was always a way to avoid the harder work. The harder work is to fill every minute, to cut without mercy, to know your text and your people well enough that the length is the right length for this passage in this room on this day. Most sermons that run long do not run long because the truth demanded it. They run long because the preacher did not do the labor of compression.

Write the sermon. Then cut it. Cut the second illustration that makes the same point as the first. Cut the recap that the people did not need. Cut the sentence you love that serves you and not them. What remains will be the right length, whatever the clock says, because it will be full.

A sermon is not measured in minutes. It is measured in whether the people met God and left changed. Get that, and no one checks their watch. Miss it, and twelve minutes is too long.
